Enquiry & quoteAdvanced5–8 weeks

Freight RFQ-to-quote with rate cards and margin approval

Read spot and contract rate requests from email, WhatsApp and tender portals, structure them, price each lane from your own buy rates, surcharges and validity dates, and give the pricing lead a draft quote to approve before it reaches the shipper.

Freight forwarding & customs

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Rate requests arrive as emails with attachments, WhatsApp messages and portal tenders, each in a different format. Pricing staff search carrier contracts, co-loader offers and surcharge notices by hand, rates expire before quotes go out, and margins vary with whoever quoted. Shippers who send the same request to several forwarders tend to book with the first complete, valid quote.

Trigger

A rate request lands in the pricing mailbox, arrives in a WhatsApp chat the shipper started, comes through the website form, or is exported from a customer tender portal.

How it runs

  1. Collect requests from the pricing mailbox, WhatsApp, web forms and tender exports into one queue, matched to existing customer accounts in the CRM.
  2. Use an AI model to extract origin and destination, Incoterm, commodity and HS code, container type or weight and volume, cargo-ready date and special handling, and list missing details as questions for the sales rep.
  3. Look up current buy rates from carrier contracts, co-loader offers and the rate sheet, add surcharges such as BAF, THC and documentation fees, and exclude rates whose validity ends before the cargo-ready date.
  4. Apply the agreed margin rules by customer tier and lane, and build a draft quote with routing options, transit times, free time, validity and exclusions.
  5. Send the draft to the pricing lead in a review screen; quotes below the margin floor go to the branch or commercial head.
  6. Send the approved quote as a PDF from the rep's address, schedule follow-ups in the CRM and record won or lost reasons by lane.

Human checkpoint

The pricing lead approves every buy rate, margin and routing before a quote is sent, and the commercial head approves anything below the margin floor or with non-standard credit terms. The automation never commits space, rates or sailings on its own.

Systems it connects

  • Freight forwarding software such as CargoWise or Magaya
  • Carrier contracts and co-loader rate sheets
  • Customer tender portals
  • CRM such as Zoho CRM or HubSpot

Data & consent

Uses business contact details and shipment particulars the shipper sent. Buy rates and margins are commercially sensitive and visible only to pricing and sales leadership; reps see sell rates. Raw emails and attachments are kept for an agreed troubleshooting period and then deleted, while approved quotes follow the client's record retention policy.

What we deliver

  • Unified rate request queue with extraction rules
  • Rate and surcharge lookup with validity checks
  • Pricing review and approval screen
  • Quote PDF template and follow-up schedule
  • Win-loss dashboard by lane and customer

How we measure it

  • Quote turnaround time
  • Quote-to-booking conversion by lane
  • Quotes sent with expired rates
  • Margin variance from the agreed matrix

Booking & pickup requestStandard4–6 weeks

Booking and pickup scheduling on WhatsApp and the portal

Let merchants book pickups through a WhatsApp Flow, the portal or an API, check serviceability, restricted items and weight before accepting, assign a pickup slot by branch cut-off, and confirm with the AWB, labels and a reminder.

Courier & last-mile delivery

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Small merchants book pickups by calling or messaging a branch, often after the daily cut-off, with incomplete addresses, wrong weights or unserviceable pin codes. Riders arrive to find parcels unpacked or not ready, missed pickups go unexplained to the merchant, and weight disputes surface later at billing.

Trigger

A merchant completes the WhatsApp booking Flow, creates a shipment in the portal, or pushes orders through the API or a connected seller platform.

How it runs

  1. Capture pickup address, ready time, number of packages, declared weight and dimensions, payment mode and declared value through a WhatsApp Flow, portal form or API.
  2. Check pin code serviceability, COD limits, prohibited and restricted items, and whether the declared value needs an e-way bill number before pickup.
  3. Create the shipment and AWB in the courier TMS, assign a pickup slot by branch cut-off and rider route, and send the merchant a confirmation with labels.
  4. Remind the merchant before the slot, and alert the branch when a rider is running late or a pickup is at risk of being missed.
  5. Record pickup scans and measured weight; when it differs from the declared weight beyond the agreed tolerance, attach dimensioner photos and notify the merchant.
  6. Send failed pickups to the branch supervisor with the reason, and offer the merchant the next available slot.

Human checkpoint

Branch supervisors approve exceptions such as pickups after cut-off, restricted items and high-value or bulk pickups. Weight disputes are decided by the billing team using the photos and dimension records, never by the automation.

Vehicle & driver assignmentStandard4–6 weeks

Driver and rider onboarding with document expiry alerts

Collect and verify driver and rider documents at onboarding, track every expiry date for licenses, registration, insurance, PUC, fitness and permits, and stop a vehicle or driver with a lapsed document from being assigned.

Fleet & road transport · Courier & last-mile delivery

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Licenses, registration certificates, insurance, PUC certificates, fitness certificates and permits expire on different dates and sit in folders, WhatsApp photos and spreadsheets. Lapses come to light at a checkpoint, during an accident claim or in a client audit. Courier networks onboarding many riders, including riders on their own two-wheelers, face the same problem at higher volume.

Trigger

A new driver or rider applies, a vehicle is added to the fleet, a document enters its reminder window before expiry, or a trip assignment is about to be confirmed.

How it runs

  1. Collect documents through a WhatsApp Flow or onboarding form after a clear notice and consent, accepting DigiLocker-issued copies the applicant chooses to share.
  2. Use OCR and an AI model to read names, numbers and expiry dates, and check license and registration details against VAHAN and SARATHI records through ULIP or an authorized verification provider.
  3. Store each document with its expiry date in a compliance register per driver and vehicle, and flag mismatches such as a license class that does not cover the vehicle type.
  4. Remind the driver, the vehicle owner and the fleet manager at agreed intervals before each expiry, and collect the renewed document in the same chat.
  5. Check validity at trip assignment and hold confirmation of any driver or vehicle with a lapsed document until the fleet manager clears it.
  6. Report upcoming expiries, lapses and renewals by branch, vendor and vehicle type.

Human checkpoint

The fleet or HR manager approves every onboarding after reviewing flagged mismatches, and decides any exception to the assignment hold. Background verification results are reviewed by a person; the AI model only reads and compares documents.

Vehicle & driver assignmentStandard3–5 weeks

Preventive maintenance and tire reminders from odometer data

Use GPS odometer readings and service history to schedule preventive maintenance, tire rotation and inspections for each vehicle, warn dispatch before a due vehicle is assigned, and track work orders to closure.

Fleet & road transport

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Service intervals are tracked in a register or in the mechanic's memory. Vehicles skip services during peak season, breakdowns strand loads mid-route, and tires and batteries are replaced without history. Dispatch cannot see which vehicles need workshop time when planning the week.

Trigger

A vehicle's GPS odometer reading crosses a service threshold, a date-based interval is reached, a driver reports a defect, or a vehicle is selected for a trip.

How it runs

  1. Pull daily odometer and engine-hour readings from the GPS or telematics platform and reconcile them with trip and fuel records.
  2. Calculate the next service, tire rotation, battery check and inspection due points for each vehicle from the maintenance plan and service history.
  3. Alert the maintenance supervisor and dispatcher as a vehicle approaches a due point, and suggest a workshop slot that fits the trip plan.
  4. Let drivers report defects with photos and voice notes on WhatsApp; an AI model turns them into structured defect reports for the supervisor.
  5. Create and track work orders with parts, cost and downtime, and mark the vehicle unavailable in the TMS until the supervisor closes the job.
  6. Report planned and unplanned maintenance, downtime and cost per kilometer by vehicle and route.

Human checkpoint

The maintenance supervisor decides whether a defect makes a vehicle unfit to run, approves any deferral of a due service and signs off completed work orders. Brake, steering, tire and other safety-related defects reported by drivers always go to a person.

Pickup, receipt & origin handlingStandard4–6 weeks

Inbound ASN-to-GRN tracking with discrepancy alerts

Match each client's advance shipping notice with the vehicle at the dock and the goods received, flag short, excess and damaged lines with photos, and send the client a GRN summary as soon as receiving closes.

Warehousing & 3PL

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Clients send ASNs as emails, spreadsheets or EDI files, and trucks arrive without appointments. Receiving teams count against printed lists, discrepancies are noted on paper, and clients learn about shortages or damage days later when stock does not show as available. Claims against suppliers and transporters then lack timely evidence.

Trigger

A client ASN arrives by EDI, API, email or the client portal, a vehicle reports at the gate, or receiving is closed for an inbound in the WMS.

How it runs

  1. Read ASNs from EDI, API, email attachments or the portal, validate SKU codes, quantities, batch and expiry fields against the client's item master, and create the expected receipt in the WMS.
  2. Offer dock appointment slots to the client or transporter, and alert the dock supervisor when a vehicle arrives without an ASN or appointment.
  3. During receiving, compare scanned quantities, batches and expiry dates with the ASN, and capture photos of damaged cartons and broken seals in the handheld app.
  4. When receiving closes, generate a GRN summary with short, excess and damaged lines and photo links, and send it to the client's nominated contacts.
  5. Open a discrepancy case for each variance with an owner and deadline, and track it until the client confirms acceptance, a return or a claim.
  6. Report dock-to-stock time and discrepancy rates by client, supplier and transporter for the weekly review.

Human checkpoint

The receiving supervisor confirms every discrepancy before the GRN summary is released, and the client's nominated contact decides whether to accept, return or claim against short or damaged goods. Quarantine and release of damaged or expired stock stay with the warehouse manager.

Each client sees only its own receipts through role-based access, and driver details are visible only to gate and dock staff.

In transit, at hubs & at customsStandard3–5 weeks

E-way bill validity watch with extension and Part B alerts

Compare each active e-way bill's validity with the vehicle's GPS position and ETA, warn the trip owner before expiry, prompt Part B updates when goods change vehicles, and prepare extension details for an authorized user to submit.

Fleet & road transport

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Trucks wait at hubs, break down or queue at consignee gates while e-way bills run out, and transshipments need Part B updated before goods move to another vehicle. Operations teams often find out when an officer stops the vehicle, and goods moving on an expired e-way bill can be detained with penalties.

Trigger

An e-way bill is linked to a trip, the GPS-based ETA moves past the validity end, the bill enters its extension window, or a vehicle change is recorded at a hub.

How it runs

  1. Read the active e-way bills for each trip through the client's GSP or ERP integration, with validity end, distance and vehicle number.
  2. Compare remaining validity with the GPS-based ETA and current position, and flag bills that will expire before delivery.
  3. Alert the trip owner when the extension window opens, with the current location, remaining distance and a draft reason, such as transshipment or accident, for the authorized user to confirm.
  4. When a vehicle change is logged at a hub, remind the hub team to update Part B with the new vehicle number before loading.
  5. Prepare the extension details for an authorized user to review and submit through the portal or API, then record the new validity on the trip.
  6. Report bills expired in transit, extensions and late Part B updates by lane, branch and customer.

Human checkpoint

An authorized user at the transporter reviews and submits every extension and Part B update. The automation never generates, extends or cancels an e-way bill on its own, and any interception or detention by officers is handled by the branch manager.

In transit, at hubs & at customsAdvanced5–8 weeks

Customs document checklist and clearance status updates

Build a document checklist for each shipment from commodity, HS code, Incoterm and destination, chase missing documents from the shipper, and keep importers and exporters updated as filing, assessment, duty payment and out of charge progress.

Freight forwarding & customs

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Clearance stalls on a missing certificate of origin, an invoice that does not match the packing list or a permit nobody asked for. Documentation teams chase shippers by email, Bills of Entry are filed late or amended, and customers call several times a day to ask whether goods are out of charge while port and CFS free time runs down.

Trigger

A shipment is booked or pre-alerted, the vessel or flight ETA changes, a document arrives, or the customs broker's filing system records a new status.

How it runs

  1. Generate a checklist for each shipment from commodity, HS code, Incoterm, origin and destination: commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading or air waybill, certificate of origin, licenses and other agency permits.
  2. Request missing documents from the shipper or consignee by email or WhatsApp, with due dates set from the arrival date and the Bill of Entry filing timeline.
  3. Use an AI model to cross-check the invoice, packing list and bill of lading for mismatched values, quantities, weights, consignee names and HS codes, and flag differences for the documentation executive.
  4. Read filing, query, assessment, duty payment and out-of-charge statuses from the customs broker's system and the ICEGATE messages it receives, and post milestones to the shipment record.
  5. Send the customer approved milestone updates, and alert the team when a query is raised or free time at the port or CFS is running out.
  6. Report clearance time, queries and amendments by port, commodity and customer.

Human checkpoint

The licensed customs broker reviews every document set, decides classification, valuation and exemption claims, and files and signs declarations on ICEGATE. AI flags mismatches but never changes a declaration, and the importer approves every duty payment.

In transit, at hubs & at customsAdvanced6–8 weeks

Proactive delay and SLA breach alerts with customer updates

Watch every shipment and warehouse order against its promised date or SLA, flag delays, stuck consignments, missed cut-offs and free-time risks early, give each exception an owner, and tell the customer before they have to ask.

Courier & last-mile delivery · Freight forwarding & customs · Warehousing & 3PL · Fleet & road transport

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Tracking data exists in the TMS, carrier portals, GPS dashboards and the WMS, but nobody watches all of it against what was promised. Delays surface when the customer calls, key accounts hear about rollovers or breakdowns late, warehouse orders miss the carrier cut-off unnoticed, and the same lanes, hubs and carriers fail repeatedly without data to show it.

Trigger

A milestone is missed or late against plan, the ETA moves past the promised date, a shipment shows no scan or GPS movement beyond the agreed limit, or an SLA timer nears breach.

How it runs

  1. Pull milestones from the TMS, courier and carrier tracking APIs, GPS platforms, WMS order status and shipping line or airline feeds into one timeline with the promised date and SLA.
  2. Run rules for missed pickups, no-movement, stuck-at-hub, ETA slippage, vessel rollovers, free-time expiry and warehouse orders not packed before the carrier cut-off, tuned per lane, service and client.
  3. Create an exception with an owner, reason code and deadline in the control-tower queue, and alert the owner in Slack.
  4. Send the consignee or shipper an approved WhatsApp, SMS or email update with the revised ETA; for key accounts, the account manager approves the message first.
  5. Escalate exceptions still open near the SLA limit to the branch or operations head.
  6. Report exceptions, causes and SLA performance by lane, hub, carrier and client for the weekly review.

Human checkpoint

Control-tower executives own every exception, confirm the reason before messages go to key accounts, and decide rerouting, upgrades and any cost or claim commitment. Customers are never promised compensation by an automated message.

In transit, at hubs & at customsAdvanced5–7 weeks

Tracking-grounded support assistant on WhatsApp and web

Answer where-is-my-shipment, delivery slot, document and stock questions on WhatsApp and web chat from live tracking and WMS data, and hand over to an agent with full context whenever a person is needed.

Courier & last-mile delivery · Freight forwarding & customs · Warehousing & 3PL

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Support teams spend much of the day reading tracking screens back to customers. Consignees ask about deliveries, importers about clearance and 3PL clients about receipts and orders. After hours nobody answers, and general chatbots that guess instead of checking the data create more calls than they save.

Trigger

A consignee, shipper or client sends a message on WhatsApp or web chat, or replies to a tracking notification.

How it runs

  1. Identify the shipment or order from the AWB, booking, container or order number, and verify the requester through the registered phone number or a one-time code before sharing details.
  2. Retrieve live status from the TMS, tracking APIs or WMS, and answer only from that data and the approved FAQ and service policies.
  3. Handle routine requests such as a delivery slot, an address landmark or a document copy within the rules set for each customer.
  4. Hand over to an agent with the conversation, shipment data and a suggested next step when the request involves a claim, damage, a refund, an address change outside the rules or an unhappy customer.
  5. Log every conversation with intent and outcome, and review a weekly sample of answers for accuracy.

Human checkpoint

Support agents handle claims, damage reports, refunds, complaints and any change to delivery terms. The assistant states only what the data shows, says so when it does not know, and sends low-confidence answers to an agent.

Delivery, NDR & proof of deliveryStandard4–6 weeks

NDR resolution with consignee re-attempt choices

When a delivery fails, confirm the reason with the consignee, offer a re-attempt date, landmark, alternate contact or self-pickup, write the choice back to the courier platform before the next dispatch plan, and flag questionable attempts for review.

Courier & last-mile delivery

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Failed deliveries come back with codes such as consignee not available, refused or address incomplete, and some are recorded without a real attempt. Merchants chase consignees by phone, re-attempt instructions arrive after the rider has left, and shipments that could have been delivered become return-to-origin costs for the merchant and the courier.

Trigger

The rider app records a failed attempt with an NDR reason code, or a consignee replies to an out-for-delivery message to say they will not be available.

How it runs

  1. Read the NDR event with reason code, attempt time, rider GPS position and call log from the courier platform.
  2. Send the consignee an approved WhatsApp template where opt-in exists, or a DLT-registered SMS, confirming the attempt and offering a re-attempt date, landmark, alternate contact, pickup point or cancellation.
  3. Capture the reply through quick-reply buttons; an AI model classifies free-text replies, and unclear ones go to an NDR agent.
  4. Write the instruction back to the courier platform before the next dispatch planning cut-off, and update the merchant through the portal or API.
  5. Flag attempts where the consignee disputes the reason, the rider's GPS position was far from the address or no call was placed, and send them to the hub supervisor.
  6. Mark shipments for return to origin only after the agreed number of attempts or on the merchant's instruction.

Human checkpoint

NDR agents handle unclear replies and disputes, hub supervisors review flagged attempts and rider conduct, and the merchant decides returns for COD and high-value shipments. Address changes to another city or pin code need the merchant's approval.

Reply logs are kept for the merchant dispute window and then deleted.

Delivery, NDR & proof of deliveryStandard4–6 weeks

Digital POD capture and freight invoice drafting

Capture proof of delivery with photos, stamp or OTP, unloading times and remarks in the driver app or on WhatsApp, match it to the LR, and turn complete PODs into draft freight invoices with detention and other charges for finance to approve.

Fleet & road transport

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Physical POD copies travel back with drivers or by courier, sometimes weeks after delivery. Billing waits for them, shippers reject invoices without a POD, detention and unloading charges go unclaimed because nobody recorded the times, and receivables stretch while finance chases paperwork.

Trigger

A driver marks a trip delivered in the app, sends a POD photo on WhatsApp, or the consignee confirms receipt with an OTP or e-signature.

How it runs

  1. Collect POD photos, consignee stamp or signature, OTP confirmation, arrival and unloading times and any shortage or damage remarks through the driver app or WhatsApp.
  2. Use OCR and an AI model to read the LR number, consignee stamp, date and remarks, match them to the trip, and flag missing stamps, unreadable images or noted shortages.
  3. Calculate freight from the contract rate card and add detention, loading, multi-point or toll charges from recorded times and the contract terms.
  4. Create a draft invoice in the accounting system with POD and LR images attached, and route it to the billing executive for review.
  5. Send approved invoices with PODs to the shipper's billing contact or portal, and track acknowledgement and payment due dates.
  6. Report POD collection time, unbilled trips and invoice disputes by customer and branch.

Human checkpoint

The billing executive reviews every draft invoice, and the finance controller approves detention or other charges outside the contract and any credit note. PODs with shortage or damage remarks go to the claims owner before billing.

COD cash and remittance reconciliation

Reconcile cash-on-delivery collections from rider cash, UPI and card payments at the doorstep against delivered AWBs, flag short deposits and mismatches daily, and prepare merchant remittance files and statements for finance to release.

Courier & last-mile delivery

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

COD money moves through riders, branch cash, bank deposits, UPI collections and payment gateways before it reaches the merchant. Finance reconciles by AWB in spreadsheets, short deposits and duplicate entries surface weeks later, and merchants chase remittances and dispute deductions because statements do not tie back to their orders.

Trigger

The daily delivery and collection export closes, a branch records a cash deposit, a bank or payment gateway settlement arrives, or a merchant remittance cycle falls due.

How it runs

  1. Pull delivered COD AWBs, rider cash collections, branch deposit records, bank statements and UPI or card settlement reports into one daily dataset.
  2. Match collections to AWBs and deposits to collections, and flag short or late deposits by rider and branch, duplicate payments and delivered COD shipments with no collection.
  3. Send branch managers a daily list of open mismatches with rider names and amounts, and track each to resolution.
  4. Build merchant remittance files for each cycle with AWB-level detail and freight and RTO deductions, and record the bank UTR against each remittance once finance releases it.
  5. Send merchants a statement with each remittance and route their disputes to the finance owner.

Human checkpoint

The finance controller approves every remittance batch before payment. Short deposits and suspected cash misuse are investigated by the branch manager and HR, never acted on by the automation, and disputed merchant deductions are held until a person decides.

Financial data about merchants and named riders, so access is limited to finance, branch managers and each merchant's own statements. Bank and gateway connections are read-only, with credentials in a secrets vault. Records follow accounting retention requirements, and rider-level discrepancy data is shared only with the people investigating it.

  • COD aging and dispute dashboard

Trip expense and fuel claims with GPS and fuel card checks

Let drivers submit fuel, toll, loading and repair expenses with receipt photos on WhatsApp, check them against fuel card, FASTag and GPS data, and give the fleet manager a short list of exceptions to approve before the trip is settled.

Fleet & road transport

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Drivers carry cash advances and return with a bundle of receipts. Accounts check them by hand against trip sheets, fuel bills do not tie to kilometers driven, toll claims overlap with FASTag deductions, and settlements drag on. Honest drivers wait for their money while questionable claims slip through.

Trigger

A driver sends an expense photo or voice note during a trip, a trip is closed in the TMS, or fuel card and FASTag statements arrive.

How it runs

  1. Collect receipts, odometer photos and voice notes from drivers on WhatsApp during the trip and attach them to the trip record.
  2. Use OCR and an AI model to extract date, amount, vendor, fuel quantity and location from each receipt, and ask the driver for anything missing.
  3. Cross-check fuel against fuel card transactions and expected consumption for the vehicle and route, tolls against FASTag statements, and claimed locations against the GPS track.
  4. Calculate the settlement against the advance and the expense policy, and list exceptions such as duplicate tolls, fuel beyond tolerance or missing receipts.
  5. Send the fleet manager the settlement with exceptions for approval, then post the approved entry to accounts and inform the driver.

Human checkpoint

The fleet manager approves every settlement and decides on exceptions after hearing the driver. Flags are prompts for a conversation, not findings of misconduct, and any deduction or disciplinary step is decided by the manager and HR.

Receipts and settlements follow accounting retention requirements, and GPS tracks used for checks are kept only for the agreed period.

  • WhatsApp expense capture for drivers
  • Receipt extraction and policy checks
  • Fuel card, FASTag and GPS cross-checks
  • Settlement approval screen with posting to accounts

  • Claims with exceptions

Client stock statements and activity-based 3PL billing

Send each 3PL client scheduled stock, ageing and near-expiry statements from the WMS, and build monthly invoices from storage, handling and value-added activity under each contract, with exceptions reviewed before finance approves.

Warehousing & 3PL

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Clients ask for stock reports in their own formats, and the warehouse team builds them by hand from WMS exports. Billing for pallet storage, inbound and outbound handling, kitting, relabeling and returns is assembled at month-end from several reports, charges are missed or disputed, and invoices go out late.

Trigger

A client's scheduled report time, month-end close, or an ad hoc statement request from a client through the portal.

How it runs

  1. Pull daily inventory snapshots and inbound, outbound, returns and value-added service logs for each client from the WMS into a warehouse data model.
  2. Send scheduled stock statements with ageing, batch, near-expiry, damaged and quarantined lines to each client's nominated contacts or portal.
  3. Calculate storage by pallet, bin or area per day and handling charges from each contract rate card, including minimum commitments and special rates.
  4. List exceptions such as activities without a rate, unusual volumes or stock held in quarantine beyond the agreed limit, and send them to the account manager.
  5. Create the draft invoice with an activity annexure for the finance controller to approve, then send both to the client.

Human checkpoint

The account manager reviews exceptions and rate questions, and the finance controller approves every invoice and credit note. Decisions on near-expiry and quarantined stock, such as liquidation, return or destruction, belong to the client and are recorded against their nominated contact.
